summary: Extends OSPF version 3 to support intra-area traffic engineering for IPv6 networks. It extends the OSPFv2 traffic engineering approach by defining a new TLV and several sub-TLVs to carry the needed link information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF is the protocol a router network uses to learn about its own links. The traffic engineering extensions to OSPF let routers also publish extra facts about those links so that paths can be planned. This RFC adds the same ability for OSPFv3, the IPv6 version of the protocol.

questions: what is the ospfv3 lsa function code for te
subtitle: Letting an IPv6 network describe its links so that paths can be planned across it.

tldr.problem: The traffic engineering extensions to OSPF were written for IPv4, so an IPv6 network had no way to publish the link information a path computation needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new OSPFv3 link state advertisement for traffic engineering, reuses the TLVs of the OSPFv2 extensions, and adds three sub-TLVs that carry the IPv6-specific identifiers and addresses.
tldr.outcome: A network running OSPFv3 can advertise its links and addresses for traffic engineering, using the same TLV format as the IPv4 version.

today: RFC 5329 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends the traffic engineering TLVs of RFC 3630 to OSPFv3 as described by RFC 5340.

sections.title: What the Document Extends
sections.content:
OSPFv3 has a very flexible mechanism for adding new link state types. Unknown types are flooded properly, based on the flooding scope bits in the link state type, so a router that does not understand a new type still passes it on. This document defines the Intra-Area-TE-LSA for OSPFv3.

For traffic engineering, the document uses the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF, RFC 3630, as the base for its TLV definitions. New TLVs and sub-TLVs are added to extend the traffic engineering capabilities to IPv6 networks, and some existing TLVs and sub-TLVs need clarification for OSPFv3 applicability. The GMPLS extensions to OSPF and the Diff-Serv MPLS extensions are themselves based on the same document, so those functions can be extended to OSPFv3 by using the TLVs and sub-TLVs described here.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocol for IPv6 already has a way to carry new kinds of information, and it already has a way to carry traffic engineering information for IPv4. This RFC joins the two: a new advertisement type for OSPFv3 that carries the IPv4-style traffic engineering information plus a few IPv6-specific additions.

sections.title: The New Advertisement and Its TLVs
sections.content:
A new link state type is defined for the Intra-Area-TE-LSA. This is different from OSPFv2 traffic engineering, where opaque link state advertisements are used to advertise traffic engineering information. The link state function code is 10, the U-bit is set, and the scope is set to 01 for area scoping. When the U-bit is set to 1, an OSPFv3 router must flood the advertisement at its defined flooding scope even if it does not recognize the type.

The Link State ID of an Intra-Area-TE-LSA is an arbitrary value used to maintain several traffic engineering advertisements. It has no topological significance.

The format of the TLVs inside the advertisement is the same as in the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF. The payload consists of one or more nested Type, Length and Value triplets, where the Type field is 16 bits, the Length field is 16 bits, and the Value holds the content. The Length field gives the length of the value portion in octets, so a TLV with no value has a length of zero. The TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the Length field: a 3-octet value has a length of 3 but the whole TLV is 8 octets. Nested TLVs are aligned the same way, so a 1-byte value has a length of 1 and 3 octets of padding are added to the end of the value. Unrecognised types are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The new advertisement is a container of typed fields, each with a type number, a length and a value. The length counts only the value, and the fields are padded so that each one starts on a four-octet boundary, which is how the nested fields line up inside it.

sections.title: What the Advertisement Carries
sections.content:
An Intra-Area-TE-LSA contains one top-level TLV, and there are two applicable top-level types: type 2, the Link TLV, and type 3, the Router IPv6 Address TLV.

The Router IPv6 Address TLV advertises a reachable IPv6 address. It is a stable address that should be reachable if there is connectivity to the OSPFv3 router. The TLV has type 3 and length 16, and its value holds a 16-octet local IPv6 address. A link-local address must not be specified in it. It must appear in exactly one traffic engineering LSA originated by an OSPFv3 router that supports the traffic engineering extensions. It is a top-level TLV as defined in the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF, and only one top-level TLV may be contained in an advertisement.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertisement carries one thing: either a description of a link, or the router's own IPv6 address so that the link can be traced back to it. That address must be one that can be reached from elsewhere, not a link-local one.

sections.title: The Link TLV and Three New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Link TLV describes a single link and consists of a set of sub-TLVs. All of the sub-TLVs of the OSPFv2 traffic engineering extensions other than the Link ID sub-TLV apply to OSPFv3. The Link ID sub-TLV cannot be used in OSPFv3, because it is defined to use the OSPFv2 identification for the designated router on multi-access networks. In OSPFv2, neighbours on point-to-point networks and virtual links are identified by their Router IDs, while neighbours on broadcast, non-broadcast multi-access and point-to-multipoint links are identified by their IPv4 interface addresses. OSPFv3 does not know those IPv4 addresses. In contrast to OSPFv2, OSPFv3 always identifies neighbouring routers by their Router IDs.

Three new sub-TLVs are defined for the Link TLV. Type 18 is the Neighbor ID, 8 octets long. Type 19 is the Local Interface IPv6 Address, 16N octets where N is the number of IPv6 addresses. Type 20 is the Remote Interface IPv6 Address, also 16N octets.
sections.plainLanguage: One top-level field describes a link and holds a set of smaller fields. Most of the smaller fields from the IPv4 version still apply. The IPv4 way of naming the far end of a link cannot be used here, so three new smaller fields replace it, carrying the neighbour's identifiers and the two addresses of the two ends.

sections.title: The Sub-TLVs in Detail
sections.content:
The Neighbor ID sub-TLV is mandatory for OSPFv3 traffic engineering support and must appear exactly once in a Link TLV. All the other sub-TLVs defined in the document should not occur more than once in a Link TLV, and if one is specified more than once the instances after the first are ignored.

In OSPFv2 the Link ID identifies the other end of a link. In OSPFv3 the combination of the neighbour's interface ID and the neighbour's router ID is used for neighbour link identification, and both are advertised in the Neighbor ID sub-TLV. The values are the same as those described in RFC 5340 for Router-LSAs. The sub-TLV has type 18 and length 8, and its value holds the neighbour's interface ID and router ID.

The Link ID sub-TLV, which is used in OSPFv2 to identify the other end of a link, should not be sent in OSPFv3 and must be ignored when received.

The Local Interface IPv6 Address sub-TLV specifies the IPv6 addresses of the interface that corresponds to this link. If several local addresses are assigned to the link, they may all be listed. Link-local addresses must not be included. The sub-TLV has type 19, and its length must always be a multiple of 16 octets, depending on the number of IPv6 global addresses advertised, with each address taking 16 octets.

The Remote Interface IPv6 Address sub-TLV advertises the IPv6 addresses associated with the neighbour's interface. It and the local address sub-TLV are used to tell parallel links between OSPFv3 routers apart. If the link type is multi-access, the remote address may be set to ::. An implementation may also choose not to send the sub-TLV at all. Link-local addresses must not be advertised in it, though neighbour addresses advertised in link-LSAs with a prefix length of 128 and the LA-bit set may be.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbour identifier is the one smaller field that must always be there, and it says both the neighbour's router identifier and its interface identifier. The two address fields list the addresses on each side of the link, and they are what tells two parallel links apart. Link-local addresses are not allowed in any of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The function described in this document does not create any new security issues for the OSPFv3 protocol. The security considerations for the base OSPFv3 protocol and for OSPFv2 traffic engineering apply to OSPFv3 traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes the security picture of the routing protocol itself; the same rules that already apply to OSPFv3 and to its IPv4 traffic engineering counterpart apply here.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
The typical management interface for routers running the new intra-area traffic engineering extensions to OSPF is SNMP based. The extra management objects for configuration operations and statistics are defined in the OSPFv3 MIB, and an implementation of the extensions in this document should provide the hooks or instrumentation that allow those MIB objects to be implemented.

Two variables have been added to the OSPFv3 MIB in support of traffic engineering. The variable ospfv3AreaTEEnabled, a TruthValue in the ospfv3AreaEntry table, says whether traffic engineering advertisement for OSPFv3 interfaces is enabled for the corresponding area, and its default value is FALSE. The variable ospfv3IfTEDisabled, a TruthValue in the ospfv3IfEntry table, says whether traffic engineering advertisement is disabled for the corresponding interface. It applies only where the area's own variable is TRUE, and its default value is FALSE as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers are managed over SNMP, and two new switches are added so an operator can turn the new advertisements on for an area and off for a single interface. Both are off by default.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: Three assignments were made from existing registries. The OSPFv3 link state type function code 10 has been assigned to the OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE-LSA. The Router IPv6 Address TLV type 3 has been assigned from the existing registry for OSPF traffic engineering TLVs. The Neighbor ID sub-TLV 18, the Local Interface IPv6 Address sub-TLV 19 and the Remote Interface IPv6 Address sub-TLV 20 have been assigned from the existing registry for OSPF traffic engineering sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA for three numbers: the code that names the new advertisement, the code for the router address field, and the codes for the three new smaller fields.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Set to 3 for the Router IPv6 Address TLV.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the value in octets, always 16.

fields.name: Router IPv6 Address
fields.desc: A stable, routable local IPv6 address. Link-local addresses are not allowed.

viz.caption: THE TYPES DEFINED OR REUSED BY RFC 5329

cells: A local IPv6 address of the router
The neighbour's interface ID and router ID
The addresses of the local interface
The addresses of the neighbour's interface

viz.caption: THE RULES THE SUB-TLVS HAVE TO FOLLOW

items.title: Neighbor ID sub-TLV
items.text: Mandatory, and it must appear exactly once in a Link TLV.

items.title: Link ID sub-TLV
items.text: Not sent in OSPFv3, and ignored when received. The Neighbor ID replaces it.

items.title: Link-local addresses
items.text: Must not appear in the router address field or in either interface address field.

items.title: Repeated sub-TLVs
items.text: Not expected; any instance after the first is ignored.

items.title: Remote address on a multi-access link
items.text: May be set to ::, or the field may be left out entirely.
